title: Better, Bolder B2B Branding: Category Entry Points in a B2B world
authors: Romaniuk, J. (LinkedIn B2B Institute / Ehrenberg-Bass Institute)
key_findings: Category entry points (CEPs) are the cues category buyers use to access memories in a buying situation.
Mental availability = being easily thought of in buying situations; more CEPs linked to a brand raise the chance it is selected (citing Romaniuk & Sharp 2000; Romaniuk 2001).
Distinctive brand assets act as memory shortcuts; assessed by fame and uniqueness (Distinctive Asset Grid).
practical_applications: List the shop's CEPs (beach glare, presbyopia onset, lost glasses on holiday) and tie each piece of content to one.
limitations: Industry paper for B2B; peer-reviewed originals not read; read via search summary.

title: Dimensions of brand personality
key_findings: As described by secondary sources: adapts the human five-factor model into a five-dimension brand personality framework; the most cited and applied brand personality scale.
practical_applications: Use the dimensions as shared team vocabulary for tone (e.g., sincerity + sophistication).
limitations: Not read this session; existence and content known only via critiques (Journal of Marketing Research).

title: Do brand personality scales really measure brand personality?
key_findings: Existing brand personality scales merge several dimensions of brand identity, personality being only one of them.
Aaker's trait selection is criticised as an all-encompassing potpourri drifting from the meaning of personality.
Other critiques question use for individual brands or within a category; a 2018 review notes the scale remains most cited.
practical_applications: Do not treat brand personality scores as precise measurement; consistency of tone matters more.
limitations: Read via abstract and secondary summaries (Journal of Brand Management 11(2):143-155).

title: The Hero and the Outlaw: Building Extraordinary Brands Through the Power of Archetypes
key_findings: Proposes 12 brand archetypes drawn from Jungian ideas; defenders say Mark used Young & Rubicam BrandAsset Valuator data (per Researchscape).
practical_applications: Use archetypes only as a character-writing aid for Mint & Tao, never as science.
limitations: Practitioner book; not read; no independent replication found.

title: Brand Archetypes (doctoral dissertation, University of Washington)
key_findings: Empirically examines Mark & Pearson's model and proposes a refined classification of the 12 archetypes into four clusters based on consumer perceptions.
Separately, a Croatian online-survey study (English abstract) found the 12 archetypes do not form unidimensional constructs.
practical_applications: Treat the 12-archetype system as unvalidated.
limitations: Read via search summary; year not confirmed; Croatian study authors not recorded.

title: How advertising works: what do we really know?
key_findings: Reviews 250+ articles and books; builds a taxonomy from no-intermediate-effects to hierarchy and non-hierarchy models.

Supports a space of intermediate effects (cognition, affect, experience) but finds little support for a fixed temporal hierarchy; AIDA-type hierarchy cannot be empirically supported (as quoted by citing work).
practical_applications: Use AIDA as a completeness checklist, not a model of how customers move.
limitations: Journal of Marketing article not read; URL is the related 1996 MSI working paper; findings via secondary summaries.

title: How advertising shapes what we think and buy (HEC Paris Knowledge@HEC summary of Valenti, Yildirim, Vanhuele, Srinivasan & Pauwels)
authors: Vanhuele, M. (summary author); study by Valenti, A.; Yildirim, G.; Vanhuele, M.; Srinivasan, S.; Pauwels, K.
key_findings: Kantar Worldpanel data: 178 FMCG brands, 18 categories, 7 years of monthly advertising, mindset and sales metrics.

Most brands show a clear dominant sequence of advertising effects; the most common is affect -> cognition -> experience (about half of brands), more prevalent for utilitarian and non-differentiated brands.
Awareness responds most to advertising; experience metrics correlate most strongly with sales; advertising has long-term effects.
practical_applications: Entertainment/affect content (Mint & Tao) can come before product information; in-store experience content matters for sales.
limitations: Business-school summary; journal and year of the underlying paper not identified; FMCG not eyewear.

title: (Article on the origin of the AIDA model) Japan Marketing History Review 3(2)
key_findings: The dominant hypothesis that E. St. Elmo Lewis invented and formulated AIDA is unsupported or based on weak evidence; stronger claims for Arthur Frederick Sheldon and Frank H. Dukesmith.
Attribution to Lewis became common after Strong's 1925 book, which dated Lewis's slogan to 1898 without naming a source.
practical_applications: Avoid repeating 'Lewis invented AIDA in 1898' as fact.
limitations: Exact title not captured; read via search summary of the J-STAGE abstract.

title: The consumer decision journey
authors: Court, D.; Elzinga, D.; Mulder, S.; Vetvik, O. J. (McKinsey Quarterly)
key_findings: Replaces the narrowing funnel with a circular journey: initial consideration, active evaluation, moment of purchase, post-purchase experience, and a loyalty loop.
A 2015 McKinsey follow-up says the journey needs updating; firms that compress or eliminate consideration/evaluation gain advantage.
practical_applications: Map the eyewear journey including post-purchase fitting and loyalty loop content.
limitations: Consulting publication; full text not read; no public quantitative validation.

title: Best practices for A/B tests in Meta Ads Manager
key_findings: Test only one variable; set a specific measurable hypothesis.
Audience large enough and not used by other concurrent campaigns (overlap contaminates results).
Run at least 7 days (up to 30); shorter tests may be inconclusive; longer if conversion lag exceeds 7 days.
Budget must produce enough results to determine a winner confidently.
practical_applications: Small shop: test big concept differences only, 7+ days, equal budget, non-overlapping audiences.
limitations: No sample-size numbers given; retrieved via Meta's official help-article tool.

title: About A/B testing for Meta ads
key_findings: A/B testing splits audiences so nobody sees both versions; measures cost per result or cost per conversion lift.
Use the same budget for both versions.
Meta does not recommend informal testing by manually turning ad sets on and off (overlapping audiences, unreliable results).
practical_applications: Use the built-in A/B tool, not on/off comparisons, before calling a winner.
limitations: Platform documentation.

title: arXiv 2305.16459 (paper on A/B test sample-size rule of thumb)
key_findings: States the widely adopted rule of thumb n ≈ 16σ²/δ² per group for α = 0.05 (two-sided) and power 0.8.
Related sources: the factor 16 rounds (z_{α/2}+z_β)² × 2; Kohavi notes it becomes about 24 at α = 0.01 (formula attributed to van Belle 2002).
practical_applications: For low base rates (e.g., 2% chat rate) detecting small lifts needs tens of thousands of people per arm; small shops should test large differences.
limitations: Preprint; title and authors not captured; read via search summary only.

title: Signaling status with luxury goods: the role of brand prominence
authors: Han, Y. J.; Nunes, J. C.; Drèze, X.
key_findings: Brand prominence = extent of visible markings that help observers recognise the brand.
Four groups by wealth and need for status: Patricians prefer quiet goods recognisable only to peers; Parvenus prefer loud; Poseurs buy loud counterfeits; Proletarians do not seek status.
Luxury brands charge more for quieter items; counterfeiters mostly copy cheaper, louder items.
practical_applications: Premium frame content: show craftsmanship details rather than enlarged logos.
limitations: Journal of Marketing 74(4):15-30; handbags, cars, shoes in Western markets; read via abstract/press/summary.

title: Subtle signals of inconspicuous consumption
key_findings: Four studies: people with domain knowledge often prefer subtle branding to differentiate from the mainstream, even though subtle markers raise misidentification risk.
Effect stronger for identity-relevant categories and more public consumption.
practical_applications: Eyewear is public and identity-relevant: understated presentation can signal premium to knowledgeable buyers.
limitations: Journal of Consumer Research 37(4):555-569; read via abstract.

title: Dark Patterns at Scale: Findings from a Crawl of 11K Shopping Websites
authors: Mathur, A.; Acar, G.; Friedman, M. J.; Lucherini, E.; Mayer, J.; Chetty, M.; Narayanan, A.
key_findings: ~53K product pages from ~11K shopping websites; 1,818 dark pattern instances on 1,254 sites (~11.1%), 15 types in 7 categories.
183 websites engaged in deceptive practices; 22 third-party entities offer dark patterns as turnkey solutions.
Develops a taxonomy of dark pattern characteristics by influence on and harm to decision-making.
practical_applications: Avoid fake scarcity, urgency timers and similar patterns in posts, chats and ads.
limitations: US-centric English shopping sites in 2019; read via abstract (attribute names not confirmed).

title: Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (FTC Staff Report)
authors: US Federal Trade Commission, Bureau of Consumer Protection
key_findings: Four groups: design elements that induce false beliefs; hide or delay disclosure of material information (e.g., drip pricing); lead to unauthorized charges; obscure or subvert privacy choices.
Appendix examples include baseless countdown timers, deceptive consumer testimonials, undisclosed paid endorsements and hidden costs/drip pricing.
Dark patterns have stronger effects when combined.
practical_applications: Use as the ethical checklist for promotions and testimonials even outside the US.
limitations: US regulator staff report, not Thai law.

title: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act), Article 25 Online interface design and organisation
authors: European Parliament and Council of the EU
key_findings: Prohibits online platform providers from designing, organising or operating interfaces that deceive or manipulate users; Recital 67 links this to dark patterns.
Applies to online platforms only; Commission may issue guidelines under Art. 25(3).
practical_applications: Reference standard for ethical interface/promotion design.
limitations: EUR-Lex not reachable; read via search summaries and a secondary legal-text site.

title: Commission Notice - Guidance on the interpretation and application of Directive 2005/29/EC (Unfair Commercial Practices Directive), C/2021/9320
key_findings: Non-binding guidance adopted December 2021 replacing the 2016 guidance; contains a dedicated section on dark patterns as unfair commercial practices deployed through interface design.
States the UCPD does not require intention for a dark pattern to be unfair (per commentary).
practical_applications: Intent does not excuse a manipulative design: judge by effect on the consumer.
limitations: Primary text not read; secondary commentary only.

title: Does Clickbait Actually Attract More Clicks? Three Clickbait Studies You Must Read
authors: Molina, M. D.; Sundar, S. S.; Rony, M. M. U.; Hassan, N.; Le, T.; Lee, D.
key_findings: Study 1 (quasi-experiment, MTurk N=149) and Study 2 (controlled experiment varying one clickbait characteristic, N=249): clickbait did not generate more curiosity than non-clickbait; participants clicked read-more/share as often or more for non-clickbait.
Study 3: four clickbait detectors agreed only 47% of the time, questioning their validity.
practical_applications: Write specific, honest hooks; curiosity gaps tied to real content, closed in the same piece.
limitations: News headlines, US online samples; read-more intention not real clicks on articles.

title: พระราชบัญญัติคุ้มครองผู้บริโภค พ.ศ. 2522 (ฉบับรวมแก้ไขถึงฉบับที่ 4 พ.ศ. 2562, สำนักงานคณะกรรมการกฤษฎีกา)
authors: Kingdom of Thailand; compiled by Office of the Council of State; hosted by Office of the Consumer Protection Board (สคบ.)
key_findings: s.3: 'ข้อความ' includes letters, pictures, film, light, sound, signs or any act making the meaning understandable.

s.22: advertising must not use statements unfair to consumers; listed as unfair: (1) false or exaggerated; (2) causing misunderstanding of material facts, whether or not citing academic reports or statistics; (3) supporting illegal/immoral acts or damaging national culture; (4) causing division; (5) others by ministerial regulation; statements the public knows cannot possibly be true are exempt from (1).

s.27: advertising committee may order amendments, bans on statements or methods, and corrective advertising; s.28: may order the advertiser to prove claims, suspend ads, and claims citing research/statistics/certification that cannot be proven are deemed false or exaggerated.

Penalties: s.47 intentional misleading advertising up to 6 months or 100,000 THB (repeat up to 1 year or 200,000 THB); s.48 up to 3 months or 60,000 THB; s.49 non-compliance with s.27/28 orders up to 6 months or 100,000 THB.
practical_applications: Keep evidence for every claim (UV400, blue-cut, 'best'); avoid health cures and unprovable superlatives.
limitations: Compilation may lag later amendments; legal interpretation not provided.

title: อย. เข้มตรวจจับ 'โฆษณาเครื่องมือแพทย์เสริมความงาม' ผิดกฎหมาย ... คุก 6 เดือน ปรับ 5 หมื่น
key_findings: Thai FDA: advertising a medical device that shows a trade name/trademark or states indications, efficacy, quality, standards, ingredients or origin requires prior FDA approval.
Approved ads must show licence number ฆพ. XX/YYYY; unlicensed advertising: up to 6 months prison or 50,000 THB fine or both; hotline 1556.
practical_applications: Contact lens content with brand names or benefit claims needs a ฆพ. number.
limitations: News report (19 Aug 2023) quoting the FDA; no statute section cited; focus on beauty devices.

title: (MGR Online news) Thai FDA: all contact lenses classified as medical devices
key_findings: Medical Device Committee resolved that all contact lenses (corrective, cosmetic, therapeutic) are medical devices under the 2008 Act, with import and sale controlled and import licences required.
practical_applications: Treat contact lens advertising as medical device advertising.
limitations: Old news (around 2009); read via search summary; current notices not checked.

title: Country Overview: Medical Devices - Thailand
key_findings: (Older scheme) Thai devices in Class I (licence), II, III; contact lenses listed among Class I licence devices; unlisted devices default to Class III.
Some products classified as devices elsewhere may not be devices in Thailand; applicants can ask the TFDA.
practical_applications: Spectacle lens/frame status must be confirmed with the Thai FDA.
limitations: Dated (around 2011-2012) and Thailand moved to risk-based classification notices in 2020; read via search summary.

title: (Thansettakij news) Ministry of Public Health drafts ministerial regulation placing eye testing for glasses under the Healthy Establishments Act
key_findings: Published 17 June 2026: draft regulation would make 'กิจการตรวจวัดสายตาประกอบแว่น' a licensed business under the Healthy Establishments Act; testers trained and registered.
Scope: refractive testing (myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, presbyopia) for ages 12+, excluding eye-muscle testing; effective 180 days after Royal Gazette publication; still a draft.
practical_applications: Monitor; future rules may affect how the shop advertises eye-testing services.
limitations: News on a draft; no advertising provisions mentioned.

title: คู่มือการคุ้มครองข้อมูลส่วนบุคคล (PDPA Guideline) incl. พระราชบัญญัติคุ้มครองข้อมูลส่วนบุคคล พ.ศ. 2562 (Royal Gazette text)
authors: Department of Intellectual Property, Ministry of Commerce, Thailand
key_findings: s.6: personal data = data identifying a person directly or indirectly (photos/video of customers qualify).
s.19: consent required unless another basis (s.24/s.26); must be explicit, in writing or electronic, purpose stated clearly in easy language, freely given, withdrawable.
s.26: sensitive data includes health data and disability -> eye prescriptions/exam results are health data.

Administrative fines: s.82 up to 1 million THB; s.83 up to 3 million THB (incl. obtaining consent by deception); s.84 up to 5 million THB (sensitive data); civil liability s.77 and punitive damages up to 2x s.78.
practical_applications: Written/chat consent form for customer photos, videos and testimonials, with separate tick for paid ads and for any health data; no prescriptions in posts.
limitations: Agency guideline for its own operations; PDPC marketing/photo guidance not read; not legal advice.

title: About Meta's health and wellness advertising policy
key_findings: No ads that imply or try to generate negative self-perception to promote health-related products.
For weight and cosmetic products/procedures: no statements of inferiority about appearance; before-and-after cosmetic transformations allowed only when targeting 18+.
No clickbait in health contexts (sensational language, extreme claims, promised outcomes in a timeframe without qualifiers); no claims to cure listed incurable diseases.
practical_applications: 'Before/after glasses' content shows experience, not shamed appearance; label vision simulations.
limitations: Platform policy can change; retrieved via official help-article tool.

title: About Meta's privacy violations and personal attributes advertising policy
key_findings: Ads must not assert or imply personal attributes of the viewer, including age, physical or mental health, medical condition and disability, including by asking questions about them.
'You/your' allowed if not tied to a prohibited attribute; Meta reports such ads lead to negative experiences and lower engagement.
practical_applications: Write 'After 40, many people...' instead of 'Are you over 40? Your eyes are failing.'
limitations: Applies to paid ads; interpretation of borderline wording is ours.

title: About Meta Advertising Standards
key_findings: Lists topic policies including personal attributes, sensational content, and personal health and appearance (no negative self-perception or unrealistic/unexpected results); ads must also follow Community Standards and commerce/branded content policies.
practical_applications: Check each paid post against the topic list before boosting.
limitations: Overview page; full policies at Meta Transparency Center not read.
